body_markdown:
Across growth-stage B2B implementations, Asure has watched the same pattern repeat. Teams spend weeks evaluating timesheet software, go live within days, then discover payroll is still running on manually reconciled exports. The tool was never the problem. The approval-to-export workflow was never designed, and that gap is where payroll accuracy breaks.


## Timesheet software solves for time visibility, and payroll accuracy is a different job


Most timesheet products on the market solve for a narrow question: where did the hours go. They show a manager a grid of clocked time, a project breakdown, or a productivity dashboard. That is a real need, and it is also a different job than making payroll accurate. Visibility tells you what happened. Payroll accuracy requires that what happened is captured, approved, and formatted in a way a payroll system can use without someone retyping it.


The content available to a buyer researching timesheet software reflects that narrow framing. Search for the best timesheet software or the best free timesheet app, and the results are dominated by feature comparisons, pricing tables, and roundups built to help someone pick between similar tools. Peer forums add opinions but rarely a framework for the decision. Almost none of it treats time capture as a payroll infrastructure decision, the kind of choice that determines whether hours reconcile cleanly at the end of a pay period or whether someone spends Thursday afternoon rebuilding a spreadsheet from timestamps.


Some teams meet time tracking for the first time as a feature bolted onto their accounting or payroll software, such as QuickBooks, rather than as a standalone decision. That framing understates the stakes. A time-tracking feature inside a broader finance tool is built to satisfy that tool's own workflow first; the approval chain and export logic a growing, multi-manager organization needs once headcount and worker types multiply is a secondary concern at best.


Asure's work with growth-stage teams consistently surfaces this misalignment. Buyers evaluate timesheet tools on interface and price, sign a contract, roll it out to employees, and only later discover that nobody defined how approved hours were supposed to reach payroll. The tool performs exactly as advertised. It just was not advertised to solve the problem that actually breaks.


The visibility-versus-accuracy gap is not random. It shows up at a specific point in the workflow, and it shows up the same way almost every time.


## The approval workflow gap is what actually breaks payroll accuracy


Capture is the easy part now. Clock-in and clock-out apps, mobile punch, calendar sync, and project-based logging have gotten genuinely good at recording when someone worked. The failure shows up one step later, when captured hours have to become approved, payroll-ready records.


Three failure modes recur across growth-stage implementations.


- **No defined approval cadence.** Without a set review window, managers often approve time in a batch at payroll close, sometimes hours before a pay run is due. Bulk, last-minute approval leaves no time to catch a missing punch, a duplicated entry, or a shift logged against the wrong pay period, so errors ride straight into the paycheck.
- **No role-based controls.** When employees can edit a record after a manager has approved it, or when there is no distinction between who can log time and who can change it, the approval itself stops meaning anything. An approved record should be locked, and an audit trail should show who touched it and when.
- **No structured export mapping.** Approved hours often live in whatever format the timesheet tool happens to use, and someone has to reformat columns, reconcile pay codes, or manually re-key totals before payroll can ingest the data, which reintroduces the manual-entry errors automation was supposed to remove.


Each gap carries a direct payroll cost. A late bulk approval produces missed overtime calculations. A record with no lock produces a dispute nobody can resolve because there is no clean version of the truth. A manual export produces the same transcription error a paper timesheet would have produced, just one step later in the process.


In Asure's work with operations and payroll leaders at growth-stage companies, the approval step gets treated as an administrative formality rather than a control point more often than any other single factor, and that's the most common source of payroll corrections Asure sees.


The stakes go beyond the operational. Under the Fair Labor Standards Act, employers must keep accurate records of hours worked for non-exempt employees, per the[U.S. Department of Labor's Fact Sheet #21 on FLSA recordkeeping requirements](https://www.dol.gov/agencies/whd/fact-sheets/21-flsa-recordkeeping) (as of 2026). An approval workflow with no lock and no audit trail does not just create payroll corrections. It creates a records gap if that data is ever questioned.


This is the part of the workflow Asure Time & Attendance is built around. Employees capture hours through the method that fits how they actually work, whether that is a clock-in and clock-out punch, a mobile app, or logging time against a project. The system flags exceptions, such as a missing punch or an unapproved overtime hour, before a manager signs off, and once hours are approved, they move into payroll without a manual reformatting step. Luna AI, embedded in AsureCentral, watches the approval queue itself rather than individual punches: if approvals are still sitting untouched as a payroll deadline closes in, it surfaces that backlog for a manager to clear before the run locks. It does not approve time on its own. It flags what needs a human decision and leaves the decision with the human, which keeps the control point where it belongs.


The approval gap gets more complicated the moment a growing company has both employees and contractors in the same system, because that combination introduces a second, separate compliance risk.


## Contractor and employee time data create two different compliance problems


The common assumption is that one timesheet system can handle every worker on the payroll, W-2 employees and 1099 contractors alike, as long as everyone logs hours somewhere. That assumption does not hold up once the compliance requirements are compared side by side.


Employee time capture exists to support wage-and-hour compliance. It is employer-controlled by design, subject to the FLSA recordkeeping standard cited above, and it feeds a payroll process that calculates withholding, overtime, and benefits accrual. Contractor time, by contrast, is typically self-reported against a project milestone, a deliverable, or an invoice, and it feeds an accounts-payable process rather than a payroll one. The two records answer different questions for different purposes.


Mixing them without role-based controls creates a specific exposure, misclassification risk. If a contractor's hours are captured, approved, and scheduled the same way an employee's are, with the same level of employer direction and control, the arrangement starts to resemble the working relationship the IRS examines when it evaluates whether someone is actually an employee. The[IRS's guidance on distinguishing independent contractors from employees](https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/independent-contractor-self-employed-or-employee) (as of 2026) weighs behavioral control, financial control, and the relationship between the parties, and a rigid, employer-directed timesheet process is exactly the kind of behavioral-control evidence that can tip that evaluation.


Practitioners already sense this. Searches for the best time tracking app for contractors show up as their own distinct cluster, separate from general employee timesheet searches, which suggests people feel the difference even without a name for it. What's missing isn't awareness. It's a framework for building two workflows where most teams are still running one.


Asure recommends that any growth-stage team with a mixed workforce, W-2 employees and 1099 contractors, treat these as two separate workflow configurations within the same platform. The role-based access built into AsureCentral supports that separation directly. A company can configure an employer-controlled approval chain and payroll export for its employees while keeping contractor self-reporting on its own track, with its own audit trail for invoice and milestone documentation, all inside one connected system.


Once the workflow is designed correctly for both worker types, the tool selection question gets much narrower, and the best-free-tool debate resolves differently than the review sites suggest.


## How to evaluate timesheet software when payroll accuracy is the goal


Once the approval-to-export workflow is mapped, evaluating software gets simpler, because most of the criteria that dominate review sites, interface polish, price per user, integration count, stop being the deciding factor. Three questions matter more.


1. **Capture method fit.** Does the capture modality match how this workforce actually works? A field crew needs mobile punch with location context. A professional services team may need project-based logging tied to client codes. A retail or hospitality team needs a fixed clock-in and clock-out. Mismatched capture methods create workaround behavior, and workarounds are where clean data breaks down first.
2. **Approval chain configurability.** Can the system enforce a defined approval sequence, lock a record once approved, and keep an audit trail of who touched it? This is the control point identified above, and it is worth testing directly during a trial rather than assuming a tool has it.
3. **Payroll export fidelity.** Does the export map directly to the destination payroll system's input format, with no manual transformation required? This is the factor free and entry-level tools most often fail once a company scales past a small headcount or adds worker-type complexity, because building a tested export mapping takes ongoing investment that a free tool's business model rarely supports.


Free and low-cost tools typically satisfy the first factor well, since capture technology has become commoditized. They partially satisfy the second factor, often with basic approval steps but limited locking or audit depth. They are least reliable on the third factor at scale, which is exactly the factor most listicle-style buying guides do not test, because doing so requires actually running a payroll cycle through the tool rather than comparing feature lists.


What Asure has seen is that teams who evaluate on these three factors, rather than on feature count or price, make a selection they don't revisit six months later when payroll corrections start accumulating.


This is the lens behind how AsureCentral is built for growth-stage teams that want to run payroll and time capture themselves. Time, HR, and payroll data share one system with role-based access, so an approved hour reaches a paycheck without a re-entry step. For a team that does not have the internal staff to design and run that workflow at all, AsureWorks is the alternative. Asure specialists manage payroll processing and coordinate time and pay data while the client remains the employer of record, with no PEO co-employment arrangement, so the operational relief doesn't cost the client any control over the workforce decisions that stay theirs.


## Bottom line


Workflow design comes first, and the tool choice follows from it. Growth-stage teams that map the approval-to-export workflow before they run a trial or issue an RFP consistently make a better tool selection and sustain payroll accuracy as headcount grows. The practical implication is straightforward: before comparing feature lists or review scores, define who approves time, on what cadence, and how approved hours are supposed to reach payroll, for both employees and any contractors on the team. The tool that fits that map is the right tool, regardless of how often it gets cited in a buying guide. Asure works with growth-stage B2B teams to design that workflow before tool selection, whether that means running it on AsureCentral or handing routine execution to Asure specialists through AsureWorks, so the implementation holds as the team scales.


## Related questions


### What is the easiest way to track employee hours accurately for payroll?


The method that produces both ease and payroll accuracy is automated time capture tied directly to an approval workflow, rather than manual entry or a free app used on its own. Employees log hours through a punch, a mobile app, or project-based entry, a manager approves within a defined window, and approved records move into payroll without manual re-entry. Ease alone breaks down at the approval and export stage, which is where most payroll corrections originate.


### What should growth-stage B2B teams look for in timesheet software?


Three factors matter most: capture method fit, approval chain configurability, and payroll export fidelity. A tool can score well on the first two and still create ongoing payroll corrections if the export does not map cleanly to the destination payroll system. Free and entry-level tools most commonly fail on export fidelity once a team scales past a small headcount.


### How is time tracking for contractors different from tracking employee hours?


Employee time capture is employer-controlled and feeds wage-and-hour payroll calculations, while contractor time is typically self-reported against a project or invoice and feeds accounts payable. Mixing the two in one workflow without role-based controls creates misclassification risk, because a rigid, employer-directed approval process can resemble the behavioral control the IRS examines when it evaluates employee status. The safer approach is two separate workflow configurations within the same platform.


### Why do timesheet implementations fail at growing companies?


The recurring pattern is tool adoption without workflow design. A company selects and rolls out timesheet software, employees start logging hours, but no one defines an approval cadence or a payroll export process, so payroll keeps running on manually reconciled spreadsheets behind the scenes. What breaks is the workflow around the tool. The software itself typically performs exactly as advertised.


### Is free timesheet software good enough for payroll compliance?


Free tools generally handle time visibility well, showing where hours went and producing basic reports. They typically fall short on audit-trail depth, role-based approval locking, and a tested payroll export, all of which matter more as headcount grows or the workforce mix includes both employees and contractors. Teams that outgrow a free tool usually notice it first as accumulating payroll corrections rather than as a missing feature.


### What is timesheet automation and how does it reduce payroll errors?


Timesheet automation replaces manual hour entry with system-generated records, such as clock-in and clock-out events, calendar integrations, or project-activity triggers, that feed an approval workflow instead of a blank form. In Asure Time & Attendance, that shift is what eliminates the transcription errors, wrong hours, missed entries, and duplicate records that accumulate at each manual handoff, since the record only gets created once, at the point of work, rather than re-keyed later by someone reconstructing it from memory.
